summary.title: Writing a Linux Debugger Part 2: Breakpoints
summary.one_liner: You learn how x86 Linux software breakpoints work (int 3 / 0xcc overwrite via ptrace) and how to implement, set, and test them in a C++ debugger.
takeaways: Software breakpoints replace the first byte of an instruction with 0xcc (int 3), which raises SIGTRAP when executed.
ptrace PEEKDATA and POKEDATA read and write whole words, so the breakpoint code saves and restores only the low byte.
The debugger uses waitpid to catch the SIGTRAP and report the stopped location.
Disabling ASLR with personality(ADDR_NO_RANDOMIZE) and reading /proc/<pid>/maps gives the load address needed to convert offsets into real breakpoint addresses.
Continuing from a breakpoint needs disabling it, single-stepping, re-enabling it, and fixing the program counter, which is deferred to the next part.
summary.summary: The article is part 2 of a series on writing a Linux debugger in C++. It explains hardware versus software breakpoints on x86, then shows how the int 3 instruction (0xcc) is written into memory using ptrace to create a breakpoint class with enable and disable methods. It adds a breakpoint map and a break command to the debugger, then covers the caveat that continuing from a breakpoint requires more work. The final section tests the breakpoints with objdump disassembly and by disabling address space randomization to find the load address via /proc/<pid>/maps.
